location.value: The Korean Peninsula, with its capital at Hanseong (Seoul).

terrain.value: A mountainous peninsula with river valleys and long coastlines.
terrain.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

climate.value: Temperate with harsh winters. Famines in 1670–71 and 1695–96 may have killed 23–33% of the population.

resources.value: Rice and other grains, ginseng, cotton and ceramics.
resources.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

population.value: About 3.3 million in 1519 and 16 million in 1889 (Wikipedia infobox). Census counts were incomplete.

urbanisation.value: Hanseong (Seoul) was the capital from 1394. Mostly rural.

disease.value: Epidemics followed famines and the 1590s wars.
disease.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

migration.value: Many Koreans were taken to Japan during the Imjin War (1592–98).
migration.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

economicBase.value: Rice agriculture, with land taxes and labour service.
economicBase.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

tradeRoutes.value: Tribute trade with Ming and Qing China. Limited trade with Japan (via Tsushima).

moneyAndTax.value: Coins (mun) were used intermittently (1423–25, 1625–1892). Taxes in grain and cloth.

inequality.value: Yangban aristocrats over commoners, “base” people and slaves (nobi), who were a large share of the population in some periods.
inequality.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy run on Neo-Confucian principles, with a State Council and Six Ministries.

keyRulers.value: Taejo (1392–1398, founder). Sejong the Great (1418–1450). Yeonsangun (deposed 1506). Jeongjo (1776–1800). Gojong (1864–1897).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Yi family, but with royal coups (e.g. Yeonsangun deposed 1506, Gwanghaegun deposed 1623).

institutions.value: Civil service examinations, the Gyeongguk daejeon law code (under Sejo), and the Six Ministries.

stability.value: Literati purges (1498–1545). Around 200 years of peace after the 1630s. Peasant revolts (e.g. the Donghak Revolution, 1894).

eliteConflict.value: Factional struggles among officials, and “sedo” politics by royal in-law families after 1800.

armyAndTech.value: Turtle ships and naval cannon under Admiral Yi Sun-sin.

majorWars.value: The Imjin War, Japanese invasions repelled with Ming help (1592–98). Manchu invasions (1627, 1636–37), which forced recognition of Qing overlordship.

territoryChange.value: Stable borders (the Yalu and Tumen rivers), set in the 15th century.
territoryChange.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

alliancesRivals.value: A loyal tributary of Ming China. Rivals: Japan and the Jurchen/Manchus.

inventions.value: Hangul, the Korean alphabet (promulgated 9 October 1446 by King Sejong), rain gauges, water clocks, and movable metal type printing.

scienceEducation.value: Sejong’s Hall of Worthies supported scholarship. Later, the Silhak (practical learning) movement.

openness.value: Became the “hermit kingdom” in the 19th century, closed to the West until forced open by Japan (1876).

communicationTransport.value: Post stations and beacon fires (bongsu) to send alarms; rivers and coastal shipping.

religion.value: Neo-Confucianism as state ideology. Buddhism was discouraged. Shamanism (musok), and Christianity (recognised 1886).

languageWriting.value: Korean (Hangul) and Classical Chinese (used by the elite).

artsArchitecture.value: Joseon white porcelain, the Gyeongbokgung palace, Hwaseong Fortress (Jeongjo), and genre painting.

socialStructure.value: Yangban, the middle class (jungin), commoners, and lowborn people and slaves (nobi).
socialStructure.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

sharedIdentity.value: Confucian culture and loyalty to the king. Korean identity was strengthened by Hangul.
sharedIdentity.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

dailyLife.value: Hanok houses with ondol (under-floor heating); rice, kimchi and soup.

neighbours.value: Ming and Qing China, Japan (Tokugawa), and the Jurchens.

ideasReligions.value: Neo-Confucian scholarship. Christianity entered via China in the 18th century.
ideasReligions.source: Seth, A Concise History of Korea (2016)

colonisation.value: Colonised. Japan forced the 1876 treaty, made Korea a protectorate (1905) and annexed it (1910).

riseSignals.value: General Yi Seong-gye took power (1388–1392) with Neo-Confucian reformers and Ming recognition.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Sejong the Great (1418–1450), the height of classical Korean culture, science and technology.

declineSignals.value: The devastating Japanese and Manchu invasions, factionalism, in-law domination, and isolation in the 19th century.

outcome.value: Transformation and colonisation. It became the Korean Empire in 1897, and was annexed by Japan in 1910.

sources.value: The Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty (very detailed), Korean, Chinese and Japanese records. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Seth (2016).

overallCertainty.value: High for events. Population figures are uncertain. Hangul is dated 1443 (creation) or 1446 (promulgation).
